newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NP hope to fade into new S.African force - de Klerk.
newsitem.headline: NP hope to fade into new S.African force - de Klerk.

text.p: Former South African president F.W. de Klerk said on Wednesday his National Party (NP), which invented apartheid, might vanish along with its name if it managed to forge a broader new political movement.

He said he was interested not in a narrow alliance with other parties opposed to President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress, but in a major political realignment in South Africa to break out of old race-based politics.
"The moderate forces in South Africa, the moderate thinkers, must find ways and means of rising above their old prejudices and taking hands," he said.
"We are identifying people who...share the same concerns with us and whom we believe share the same values."

His still white-dominated NP, which implemented apartheid but dismantled it four decades later and yielded to all-race elections in 1994, has said it must do more to win votes from the black majority if it is to remain a major force.

De Klerk said he hoped the "Nats" and others who share its conservative, free-market and pro-family values would get a new movement off the ground this year, ready to fight the 1999 elections which he says he wants to win.

"If we're sure such a new entity of which we become part will be stronger than us, be built on our values, have cohesion and not split apart in six months," he said, "we would under such circumstances be prepared to stop existing as we are."

But de Klerk, who shared the 1993 Nobel peace prize with Nelson Mandela, now president, said that the NP would keep its name until it was convinced the movement it would disappear into represented something really new.
"Simply a change of name will not bluff anybody," he said.
His party was voted in by the white electorate after World War Two and embarked on its notorious policy of racial segregation that ensured white supremacy.

De Klerk started to dismantle apartheid after he took over from ailing president P.W. Botha in 1989 and, highlighting how the party had reformed under him, pointed out on Wednesday that all race laws had been abolished by the time Mandela took over.
The NP quit Mandela's unity government last year, saying its views were being ignored.
